file.content: Self-Consistency (SC) majority voting over multiple chain-of-thought traces is the dominant test-time aggregation strategy for large language models (LLMs), but accuracy gains saturate as sample count grows. The Condorcet Jury Theorem (CJT) explains this plateau: same-model traces are correlated voters, so additional samples carry diminishing independent information. Symbolic constraints expressed in first-order logic (FOL) appear to offer a way forward, since formal validity is independent of the generative model. Yet when constraints are extracted by the same model that produces the traces, they inherit the traces' correlation structure. We term this the \emph{independence bottleneck}. We study this bottleneck through Symbolic Invariant Consensus Aggregation (SICA), which extracts FOL constraints from reasoning traces and selects answers via weighted partial MAX-SAT. Evaluating six models (7B to 32B parameters) across three reasoning domains with over 3,000 instances and four-seed replication, we find a regime-dependent pattern: positive directional trends ($p < 0.10$ in 2 of 4 seeds, none reaching $p < 0.05$; best seed $+3.43$\,pp, 4-seed mean $+1.47$\,pp) occur only in a narrow band around 50 to 55\% SC baseline on a highly formalizable domain (one model, one dataset). Outside this zone, constraints either echo the majority (confirmation bias) or amplify errors. Cross-model entropy decomposition reveals the mechanism: all SICA effects concentrate in high-entropy problems, but the direction depends on the accuracy regime. Oracle controls with gold FOL annotations confirm the aggregation mechanism is sound, yet self-extraction captures only 24\% of the oracle ceiling. Nine remediation strategies spanning six intervention dimensions all fail to widen the effective zone. The bottleneck is structural: same-model self-extraction cannot supply the independent signal that CJT requires for aggregation to surpass majority voting.
